prompt.context: Your client is a grocery store that primarily operates in the southern US. Your point of contact works in the beverage department which consists of carbonated beverages (soda), non-carbonated beverages, and water. Revenue has been dropping in the last two years, specifically in carbonated beverages.
prompt.question: How would you recommend improving the performance of carbonated beverages?

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal — revenue improvement only or overall profitability?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is profitability, not just revenue.

clarifying_info.q: By how much has revenue fallen?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue fell 1% two years ago and 3% last year.
Pricing has been stable and in line with competitors, which indicates the decline is driven by lower volume.

clarifying_info.q: Which brands does the client carry in carbonated beverages?
clarifying_info.a: Coke, Pepsi, Dr. Pepper, Boylan's (a craft brand), and a Store Brand.

clarifying_info.q: Where are carbonated beverages currently sold in the store?
clarifying_info.a: Currently just in the beverage aisle. Could also be sold on end-caps, coolers by the registers, or out front of the store.

clarifying_info.q: Is there brand loyalty among customers?
clarifying_info.a: A large majority of Coke drinkers will always choose Coke. The same goes for Pepsi and Dr. Pepper.

exhibits.title: Beverage Brand Revenue, Cost, and Volume
exhibits.shows: A table listing each carbonated beverage brand with its per-case revenue, per-case cost, and number of cases sold.

framework: Company — analyze beverage department profitability: revenue mix across brands (volume and price), costs per brand, and contribution from the full store
Customers — assess price sensitivity, brand loyalty, and taste/purchasing trends driving volume decline
Market — evaluate whether carbonated beverage category is growing or declining and where competitors stand
Revenue levers — identify ways to increase volume: promotions, store placement (end-caps, coolers at registers, storefront), and brand mix optimization

questions.prompt: Now that you have seen the volume and margins of each brand (Exhibit 1), which brand would you recommend the client focus on to increase revenue and profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate margin per case for each brand and compare: Coke $0.50, Pepsi $0.75, Dr. Pepper $0.75, Boylan's $2.00, Store Brand $1.00. A strong answer identifies the Store Brand: it has the highest margin per case among accessible-volume brands (2x Coke's margin per case), lower current volume suggesting room to grow, and because major-brand drinkers are highly loyal, promotions targeting those customers are unlikely to convert them — new soda purchasers are best captured with the store brand.

questions.prompt: A) What percentage of total store carbonated beverage profit comes from the Store Brand? B) How many total cases of the Store Brand would the client need to sell so that its profit equals the profit from the most profitable brand? C) Is increasing Store Brand sales by an additional 1,000 cases a reasonable goal?
questions.guidance: A) Candidate must compute profit per brand then find Store Brand share. B) Identify most profitable brand (Dr. Pepper at $6K), then solve for cases needed at $1 margin. C) Candidate should comment that a ~20% volume increase is not trivial and requires a concrete strategy.

math.setup: Margin per case = Revenue per case - Cost per case. Profit per brand = Margin * Cases. Total profit = sum of all brands.
steps: B) Most profitable brand = Dr. Pepper at $6,000. Store Brand needs $6,000 / $1.00 = 6,000 cases, i.e. 1,000 additional cases.
C) 1,000 additional cases = ~20% volume increase for the Store Brand; not realistic without a specific expansion strategy.
math.answer: A) ~21.5%; B) 6,000 total cases (1,000 additional); C) A 20% volume increase is aggressive and requires a concrete plan.

questions.prompt: What are some ways the grocery store can increase sales of the Store Brand?
questions.guidance: This is an open brainstorm. Strong answers are structured (e.g., Product vs. Marketing buckets) and generate multiple concrete ideas per category.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways the grocery store can increase sales of the Store Brand carbonated beverage?

categories.name: Product
ideas: Improve the recipe based on customer feedback
Expand store brand to adjacent categories (food, snacks, juices)

categories.name: Marketing & Placement
ideas: Run taste tests to build awareness and loyalty

recommendation: Focus on the Store Brand carbonated beverage, which carries the highest per-case margin and has the most room for volume growth among customers who are not loyal to a name brand.
risks: Cannibalization: promotions may pull the small fraction of non-loyal Coke/Pepsi drinkers to the store brand, increasing margin but not necessarily total revenue if volume simply shifts rather than grows.
next_steps: Determine the best promotion and marketing approach for the store brand (pricing, packaging, tastings).
Optimize store placement (end-caps, checkout coolers, storefront display) to drive trial.
Run taste tests to improve product quality and increase repeat purchase.
